Code]] | postal_code = 11377 | area_code_type = [[Telephone numbering plan|Area code]]s | area_code = [[Area codes 718, 347, and 929|718, 347, 929]], and [[Area code 917|917]] }} '''Woodside''' is a neighborhood in the western portion of the [[borough (New York City)|borough]] of [[Queens]] in [[New York City]]. It is bordered on the south by [[Maspeth, Queens|Maspeth]], on the north by [[Astoria, Queens|Astoria]], on the west by [[Sunnyside, Queens|Sunnyside]], and on the east by [[Elmhurst, Queens|Elmhurst]], [[Jackson Heights, Queens|Jackson Heights]], and [[East Elmhurst, Queens|East Elmhurst]]. Some areas are widely residential and very quiet, while other parts, especially the ones around [[Roosevelt Avenue]], are busier. In the 19th century the area was part of the Town of Newtown (now [[Elmhurst, Queens|Elmhurst]]). The adjacent area of Winfield was largely incorporated into the post office serving Woodside and as a consequence Winfield lost much of its identity distinct from Woodside. However, with large-scale residential development in the 1860s, Woodside became the largest [[Irish American]] community in Queens, being approximately 80% Irish by the 1930s and maintaining a strong Irish culture today. In the early 1990s, many [[Asian American]] families include a large [[Filipinos in the New York metropolitan area|Filipino community]] moved into the area, and as a result the current population is 30% Asian American. [[South Asian]]s and [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Latino]]s have also moved to Woodside in recent years. Reflecting the neighborhood’s long-standing cultural diversity, the area offers a wide range of international restaurants, cafés, and pubs. It is particularly known for its [[Thai food|Thai]], [[Filipino food|Filipino]], and [[Cuisine of South America|South American]] dining options, which contribute to the neighborhood’s varied and distinctive culinary scene.{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2004/11/03/dining/a-thai-pilgrimage-leads-to-queens.html |title=A Thai Pilgrimage Leads to Queens |last=Bruni |first=Frank |date=November 3, 2004 |work=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 |access-date=January 22, 2019 |language=en-US |archive-date=January 22, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190122145034/https://www.nytimes.com/2004/11/03/dining/a-thai-pilgrimage-leads-to-queens.html |url-status=live }}{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/02/15/nyregion/thecity/15joll.html |title=Filipino "Soul Food" Comes to Queens |last=Foggin |first=Mark |date=February 13, 2009 |work=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 |access-date=January 22, 2019 |language=en-US |archive-date=January 22, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190122145006/https://www.nytimes.com/2009/02/15/nyregion/thecity/15joll.html |url-status=live }}Woodside is located in [[Queens Community Board 2|Queens Community District 2]] and its ZIP Code is 11377. It is patrolled by the [[New York City Police Department]]'s 108th Precinct. Politically, Woodside is represented by the [[New York City Council]]'s 22nd and 26th Districts.[http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/queens.pdf Current City Council Districts for Queens County] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161222003335/http://www.nyc.gov/html/dc/downloads/pdf/queens.pdf |date=December 22, 2016 }}, [[New York City]]. The "Great Chestnut Tree" was actually located on the west side of the road where it is shown. {{hidden end}} ]] For two centuries following the arrival of settlers from England and the [[Netherlands]], the area where the village of Woodside would be established was sparsely populated. The land was fertile, but also wet. Its Native American inhabitants called it a place of "bad waters", and it was known to early European settlers as a place of "marshes, muddy flats and bogs", where "wooded swamps" and "flaggy pools" were fed by flowing springs."{{Cite web |url=http://www.maspethchamberofcommerce.org/maspeth.htm |title=History of Maspeth |publisher=Maspeth Chamber of Commerce |access-date=March 22, 2013 |archive-date=March 4, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304075648/http://www.maspethchamberofcommerce.org/maspeth.htm |url-status=dead }}{{cite book |url=https://archive.org/details/algonquianseries02tookrich |title=The Algonquian series |author=William Wallace Tooker |publisher=F.P. Harper |year=1901 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/algonquianseries02tookrich/page/40 40]– |access-date=January 5, 2013}} Until drained in the nineteenth century, one of these wet woodlands was called Wolf Swamp after the predators that infested it.{{cite news |url=http://www.fultonhistory.com/Newspaper4/Newtown%20NY%20Register/Newtown%20NY%20Register%201898%20Jan-Apr%201899%20Grayscale/Newtown%20NY%20Register%201898%20Jan-Apr%201899%20Grayscale%20-%200106.pdf#xml=http://www.fultonhistory.com/dtSearch/dtisapi6.dll?cmd=getpdfhits&u=4921a96b&DocId=1363242&Index=Z%3a\Index%20O-G-T&HitCount=3&hits=a4+a5+c9b+&SearchForm=C%3a\inetpub\wwwroot\Fulton_New_form.html&.pdf |title=Ancient Newtown, Formerly Middleburg. Seyfried |author2=William Asadorian |publisher=Courier Dover Publications |year=1991 |isbn=978-0-486-26358-8 |pages=66– |access-date=February 15, 2013}} This swamp was not the only place where settlers might fear for the safety of their livestock, and even themselves. One of the oldest recorded locations in Woodside was called Rattlesnake Spring on the property of a Captain Bryan Newton. The vicinity came to be called ''Snake Woods,'' and one source maintains that "during New York's colonial period, the area was known as 'suicide's paradise,' as it was largely snake-infested swamps and wolf-ridden woodlands."{{Cite web |url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/about/history/historical-signs/listings?id=12766 |title=Woodside Plaza |work=City of New York Parks & Recreation Historical Signs Project |access-date=January 10, 2013 |archive-date=February 4, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120204102830/http://www.nycgovparks.org/about/history/historical-signs/listings?id=12766 |url-status=live }} Woodside was settled by farmers in the early 18th century.{{cite news |url=http://longislandgenealogy.com/KellyFamily/Woodside%20History.pdf |title=Woodside of Long Ago! |author=Margaret E. Brennan |date=March 1983 |newspaper=Woodsider |access-date=January 30, 2012 |issue=8 |volume=6}} In time, inhabitants learned how to farm the land profitably. The marsh grasses proved to be good for grazing and grains, fruits, and vegetables could be grown on the surrounding dry land. By the middle of the 18th century, the area's farmers had drained some of its marshes and cut back some of its woods to expand its arable land and eliminate natural predators. Agricultural produce found markets in New York City, and at the beginning of the 19th century the area came to be "abundantly conspicuous in the wealth of the farmers and in the beauty of the villas." A late 19th-century historian described one of the area's 19th-century farms as a pleasing mix of woodlot, tilled acreage, grazing land, orchard, and pleasure garden. He believed "it would probably have been hard to find anywhere in the vicinity of New York a more picturesque locality."{{cite news |url=http://www.fultonhistory.com/Newspaper4/Newtown%20NY%20Register/Newtown%20NY%20Register%201898%20Jan-Apr%201899%20Grayscale/Newtown%20NY%20Register%201898%20Jan-Apr%201899%20Grayscale%20-%200098.pdf#xml=http://www.fultonhistory.com/dtSearch/dtisapi6.dll?cmd=getpdfhits&u=ffffffffbfc8bf70&DocId=1363234&Index=Z%3a\Index%20O-G-T&HitCount=5&hits=ce+18b+18c+18d+b13+&SearchForm=C%3a\inetpub\wwwroot\Fulton_New_form.html&.pdf |title=Ancient Newtown, Formerly Middleburg. Article 9, The Woodward or Meyer Farm--Shaw's Hotel—The William Leverich Homestead—The John Sackett Farm and Woodside |author=J.H. Innes |date=March 17, 1898 |work=Newtown Register |archive-date=September 24, 2015 |access-date=September 9, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924043022/http://www.fultonhistory.com/Newspaper4/Newtown%20NY%20Register/Newtown%20NY%20Register%201898%20Jan-Apr%201899%20Grayscale/Newtown%20NY%20Register%201898%20Jan-Apr%201899%20Grayscale%20-%200098.pdf#xml=http://www.fultonhistory.com/dtSearch/dtisapi6.dll?cmd=getpdfhits&u=ffffffffbfc8bf70&DocId=1363234&Index=Z%3a\Index%20O-G-T&HitCount=5&hits=ce+18b+18c+18d+b13+&SearchForm=C%3a\inetpub\wwwroot\Fulton_New_form.html&.pdf |url-status=live }} Another observer of this time praised Woodside's "pure atmosphere and delightful scenery."{{cite book |url=http://www.bklyn-genealogy-info.com/Queens/history/newtown.html |title=Remains of Ancient Newtown in HISTORY OF QUEENS COUNTY with illustrations, Portraits & Sketches of Prominent Families and Individuals |last=O'Gorman |first=William |publisher=W.W. Munsell & Co. |year=1882 |location=New York |pages=329–408 |archive-date=May 10, 2015 |access-date=September 9, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150510105513/http://www.bklyn-genealogy-info.com/Queens/history/newtown.html |url-status=live }} In the 19th century, the area was part of the Town of Newtown (now [[Elmhurst, Queens|Elmhurst]]). The adjacent area of Winfield was largely incorporated into the post office serving Woodside and as a consequence Winfield lost much of its identity distinct from Woodside. Some idea of the bucolic nature of the place that would become Woodside can be seen in descriptions of an ancient central landmark, a great chestnut tree. The tree was hundreds of years old when it finally came down in the last decade of the 19th century. It stood on high ground near a junction of three dirt roads and "was of great diameter, some 8 or 10 feet"—perhaps 30 feet in circumference.{{cite news |url=http://www.fultonhistory.com/Newspaper%204/Newtown%20NY%20Register/Newtown%20NY%20Register%201887%20Jan-Jun%201888%20Grayscale/Newtown%20NY%20Register%201887%20Jan-Jun%201888%20Grayscale%20-%200445.pdf#xml=http://www.fultonhistory.com/dtSearch/dtisapi6.dll?cmd=getpdfhits&u=ffffffffd4ec7dcd&DocId=6355548&Index=Z%3a%2fFulton%20Historical&HitCount=7&hits=50e+9b4+9b5+1581+1582+1781+1782+&SearchForm=C%3a\inetpub\wwwroot\Fulton_New_form.html&.pdf |title=Old Newtown and Its Confines, Selections from the Town Scrap book, The Old Chestnut Tree of Woodside. – The Hallett Murder |author1=William O'Gorman |date=January 12, 1888 |work=Newtown Register |author2=Town Clerk |archive-date=September 24, 2015 |access-date=September 9, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924020758/http://www.fultonhistory.com/Newspaper%204/Newtown%20NY%20Register/Newtown%20NY%20Register%201887%20Jan-Jun%201888%20Grayscale/Newtown%20NY%20Register%201887%20Jan-Jun%201888%20Grayscale%20-%200445.pdf#xml=http://www.fultonhistory.com/dtSearch/dtisapi6.dll?cmd=getpdfhits&u=ffffffffd4ec7dcd&DocId=6355548&Index=Z%3a%2fFulton%20Historical&HitCount=7&hits=50e+9b4+9b5+1581+1582+1781+1782+&SearchForm=C%3a\inetpub\wwwroot\Fulton_New_form.html&.pdf |url-status=live }} Its size and central location made it a natural meeting place, its surface one on which to tack public notices, and a strategic point of considerable military significance during the Revolutionary War. A 19th-century antiquarian wrote of the great tree as it stood during the American Revolution and in doing so named the families of the local landowners:
Around the roots of the old tree were the huts and stables of the cavalry: with a number of settler's huts ranged in woods... Great festivities too were constant in the spacious rooms of the old Moore house, during the winter months when the snow was deeper and the frost more cold than now-a-days. To the streaming lights from the ball room, and the lanterns hung on the trees, were wont to assemble the gay sleighing parties from the Sacket [i.e. Sackett], Morrell, Alsop, Leverich and other houses; for the soldiers were all over and had come to Newtown to recruit [i.e. refresh and restore] themselves after the yearly campaigns... Is there any relic more associated with Newtown [i.e. the town in which the village of Woodside would come to be located] than its old chestnut tree?... [Has it] not been for two centuries the "Legal Notice" centre of Newtown, for all vendues, real estate transfers, town meetings, lost "creeturs" and runaway slaves?
Woodside was first developed on a large scale beginning in 1867 by speculative residential neighborhood builder Benjamin W. Hitchcock, who also founded [[Corona, Queens|Corona]] and [[Ozone Park, Queens|Ozone Park]], and John Andrew Kelly.{{cite web |url=http://www.queenslibrary.org/index.aspx?page_nm=CL-Communityinfo&branch_id=Ws |title='queens Library Community and Library History (Woodside) |publisher=Queens Public Library |access-date=January 30, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111014093213/http://queenslibrary.org/index.aspx?page_nm=CL-CommunityInfo&branch_id=Ws |archive-date=October 14, 2011 |url-status=dead }} The neighborhood's location about three miles from Hunter's Point on the [[Long Island Rail Road]] line made it an ideal location for a new suburban community. In 1874, the ''New York Times'' described Woodside: {{Blockquote|At Woodside there are now 100 houses erected, chiefly of the villa-cottage order, and thirty trains daily stop at the station, making it, via the Hunter's Point and James Slip Ferry, less than forty-five minutes from the lower part of the city. Woodside is located on sloping ground, having a good elevation, and pleasing, though not very diversified scenery. There is an abundance of good fruit trees in the vicinity...{{cite web |title=LONG ISLAND.; POPULAR LOCALITIES NEAR NEW-YORK THEIR GROWTH, AND HOW TO GET TO THEM. |newspaper=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 |date=June 27, 2019 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1874/05/31/archives/long-island-popular-localities-near-newyork-their-growth-and-how-to.html |access-date=July 8, 2019 |archive-date=July 8, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190708171253/https://www.nytimes.com/1874/05/31/archives/long-island-popular-localities-near-newyork-their-growth-and-how-to.html |url-status=live }}}} ====Agriculture==== By the middle of the 19th century, drainage and improved agricultural techniques had increased the proportion of Woodside's arable land to some two-thirds of its total. Flowers and dairy products were added to the fruits and vegetables which farmers took to city markets. These landowners also reaped benefits from improved transportation. Mid-century construction of a plank road from Newtown to [[Williamsburg, Brooklyn|Williamsburg]] and a later one from Newtown to [[Hunters Point, Queens|Hunters Point]] made access to [[List of ferries across the East River|East River ferries]] quicker and easier.{{cite journal |year=1866 |title=An Act to provide for laying out, opening and grading a public road or highway in the town of Newtown, Queens county |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Xmw4AAAAIAAJ&q=%22plank+road%22+newtown+queens&pg=PA1476 |journal=Laws of the State of New York Passed at the 89th Session of the Legislature, Vol. II |issue=April|last1=(State) |first1=New York }} In 1860 a corporation presided over by a local resident, John C. Jackson, built a gravel-topped toll road between [[Flushing, Queens|Flushing]] and the ferry at Hunters Point.{{Cite web |url=http://newtownpentacle.com/2009/08/17/astoria-zen/ |title=Astoria Zen: Part One of a photowalk, Lords and Ladies of Newtown, from Astoria to Calvary |work=Newtown Pentacle |date=August 17, 2009 |access-date=January 21, 2013 |archive-date=October 30, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121030171854/http://newtownpentacle.com/2009/08/17/astoria-zen/ |url-status=live }} The Plank Road disappeared during construction projects of the later 19th century but [[New York State Route 25A|Northern Boulevard]] tracks closely resemble the route of Jackson Avenue.{{Cite web |url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/Q232/history |title=Dwyer Square |work=New York City Parks. Historical Signs Project |publisher=City of New York. Parks and Recreation |access-date=January 21, 2013}}{{Cite web |url=http://stsebastianwoodside.org/history.htm |title=The History of St. Sebastian Parish: 1894-1994 |year=2009 |work=St. Sebastian Roman Catholic Church |access-date=January 19, 2013 |archive-date=February 16, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130216024201/http://stsebastianwoodside.org/history.htm |url-status=live }}{{cite news |url=http://longislandgenealogy.com/KellyFamily/Woodside%20History.pdf |title=Woodside Long Ago |author=Margaret E. Brennan |date=March 1983 |work=Woodsider |issue=8 |volume=6 |archive-date=December 10, 2011 |access-date=January 30, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111210021921/http://longislandgenealogy.com/KellyFamily/Woodside%20History.pdf |url-status=live }} ====Residential estates==== [[File:HillsideManorHouseAtWoodside.jpg|thumb|left|A decayed tintype, showing Hillside Manor in the 1870s. {{hidden begin|title=More details}} The house, sited on high point not far from the Great Chestnut Tree in Woodside, lay on nine acres of land with gardens laid out by [[Frederick Law Olmsted]]. Owned by Louis Windmuller, German immigrant, New York merchant, financier, and philanthropist, the estate was one of the last in Woodside to be sold for development. In 1936 the city acquired most of the property for a park to be called Windmuller Park and in 1942 the heirs sold the remainder to a developer for construction of [[garden apartment]]s. {{hidden end}} ]] The improvements in transportation that initially benefited agriculture eventually led to its decline. As it became quicker and more convenient for residents to travel from their homes to other parts of Queens, to Brooklyn, and to Manhattan, the area came to be seen as both desirable and affordable for the construction of housing for city-dwellers and increases in land values enticed farm owners to sell out. John Sackett came from a family of religious [[dissenter]]s that had settled in Queens late in the 17th century. In 1802 he inherited a farm of 115 acres including much of what is now Woodside, and in 1826 his heirs sold much of the property to John A. Kelly, the son of a German immigrant, and his sister-in-law (also of German descent), Catherine B. (Friedle) Buddy.{{Cite web |url=http://longislandgenealogy.com/SackettKelly.html |title=The History of the Sackett/Kelly/Howell Estate |author=Owen Clough |access-date=February 12, 2013 |archive-date=March 12, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130312071620/http://longislandgenealogy.com/SackettKelly.html |url-status=live }} As other well-to-do merchants had done in other areas of Queens, Kelly and Buddy bought farm property for use as a rural estate where they planned to live in the warmer months of the year.{{cite journal |author=William O'Gorman |year=1882 |title=Remains of Ancient Newtown: Woodside |url=http://www.bklyn-genealogy-info.com/Queens/history/newtown.html |journal=In: History of Queens County, with Illustrations, Portraits, & Sketches of Prominent Families and Individuals (New York, Munsell & Co) |pages=329–408 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090220003729/http://www.bklyn-genealogy-info.com/Queens/history/newtown.html |archive-date=2009-02-20}} Not long after, a friend of Kelly's, William Schroeder, bought another parcel of the Sackett property for the same purpose. Like Kelly, he came of a family that had emigrated from Germany and, like Kelly, he had achieved wealth as a merchant in [[Charleston, South Carolina]]. Unlike Kelly, however, he did not move North, but kept the estate for use during summer vacations. After Kelly and Schroeder had moved in, two other well-to-do men of German extraction made country retreats for themselves in Woodside. They were Gustav Sussdorf and Louis Windmuller. Like Kelly and Schroeder, Sussdorf was a Charleston merchant. In 1859 he sold his fancy goods business and moved to New York.{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=GHBfBOdwsCkC |title=The Buildings of Charleston: A Guide to the City's Architecte |author=Jonathan H. Poston |publisher=Univ of South Carolina Press |year=1997 |isbn=978-1-57003-202-8 |access-date=February 13, 2013}}{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8oUtAAAAYAAJ |title=Trow's New York City Directory |publisher=J. F. Trow. |year=1859 |access-date=February 13, 2013}} Not long after, he bought a farm owned by the family of Thomas Cumberson who had died in 1849. It is quite possible that he learned of the place through acquaintance with Schroeder or, more likely, Kelly.{{Cite web |url=http://longislandgenealogy.com/Cumberson.html |title=Cumberson Burying Ground - 1829-1849 |publisher=Long Island Genealogy |access-date=February 15, 2013 |archive-date=February 22, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140222205931/http://longislandgenealogy.com/Cumberson.html |url-status=live }} Windmuller was of a younger generation than Kelly, Schroeder, and Sussdorf. He emigrated to New York in the aftermath of the [[Revolutions of 1848]]. Only 18 years old and penniless, he found success as a commission agent, bringing goods to clients in the U.S. from Germany and other European countries. In 1867 he had accumulated enough savings to buy property adjoining Sussdorf's. The land had formerly belonged to the Morrell family, but had been acquired by a speculator, John A. Mecke, and became available to Windmuller upon Mecke's death and the bankruptcy of his estate.{{efn|For succinct accounts about Sussdorf and Windmuller see ''Woodside: A Historical Perspective 1652-1994'' by Catherine Gregory (Woodside on the Move, 1994). A descendant of Windmuller's has written extensively about him and his life in Woodside. Idell |year=1899 |publisher=D. Appleton and Co.}} Founded in 1854, Winfield is a neighborhood in eastern Woodside. The place known as "suicide's paradise" lay on the west side of the neighborhood. The photo shows that Woodside retained some portion of its rural character even at the end of the 19th century. {{hidden end}} ]] As farms gave way to [[country estate]]s, so country estates would, in turn, give way to residential development, as, in the decades after 1850, the land was broken into small lots for construction of single-family houses. As before, this new shift was brought about largely by improvement in transportation resources. In 1854, the first steam-powered passenger rail service came to the area. In that year a passenger depot of the Flushing Railroad from Long Island City to Flushing opened for operation near the southern boundary of what would become the village of Woodside. The line gave access to New York City via the Hunters Point Ferry and to Brooklyn via horse-drawn omnibus.{{Cite web |url=http://arrts-arrchives.com/pennybridge.html |title=The Flushing Rail Road Company and Penny Bridge Station |author=John Huneke |year=2010 |work=Arrt's Arrchives |access-date=January 17, 2013 |archive-date=August 13, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120813035354/http://arrts-arrchives.com/pennybridge.html |url-status=live }} In 1861 a second line opened running directly through what would shortly become the village of Woodside. This was a segment of the [[Long Island Rail Road]] which operated between Hunters Point and [[Jamaica, Queens|Jamaica]], replacing an earlier segment which passed through Brooklyn to the ferry dock in Williamsburg.{{Cite web |url=http://www.lirrhistory.com/timeline.html |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20011215072407/http://lirrhistory.com/timeline.html |url-status=dead |archive-date=December 15, 2001 |title=LIRR Timeline |author=Robert W. The area that would become Woodside was not the first community to grow out of Queens farmland. Before the end of the 1850s Woodhaven, [[Astoria, Queens|Astoria]], [[Maspeth, Queens|Maspeth]], Corona, Hunters Point, and Winfield all attracted land speculators.{{Cite web |url=http://www.queensbp.org/content_web/tourism/tourism_history.shtml |title=A Brief History of Queens |work=Queens Borough |publisher=Borough of Queens [official site] |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071218014547/http://www.queensbp.org/content_web/tourism/tourism_history.shtml |archive-date=December 18, 2007 |url-status=dead |access-date=January 16, 2013}}{{Cite web |url=http://www.thirteen.org/queens/history2.html |title=Queens, History: Birth of a Borough |author=Barry Lewis |work=A Walk Through Queens |publisher=Educational Broadcasting Corporation |access-date=January 17, 2013 |archive-date=September 24, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120924002742/http://www.thirteen.org/queens/history2.html |url-status=live }} Woodside's developers were, however, among the first to divide properties into lots for construction of small homes for working-class families. In doing so they were the first to use a set of new sales techniques to lure buyers. And they were the first to apply a name to a locale which emphasized its real or supposed virtues. A late 19th century author said "Woodside" was an appropriate name for the community these land speculators created. He maintained that others, created later, were "without the slightest significance, historic or otherwise, and of the kind apparently chosen by boarding schoolgirls to roll romantically from the tongue.". These included [[Ozone Park, Queens|Ozone Park]], [[Corona, Queens|Corona]], [[Winfield, Queens|Winfield]], [[Glendale, Queens|Glendale]], Laurel Hill, Elmhurst, and [[Linden Hill, Queens|Linden Hill]]. The real estate promoters who created Woodside were mostly of German extraction. Members of the Kelly family were first, followed by Alpheus P. Riker, Henry G. Schmidt, John A. Mecke, and Emil Cuntz. The Kelly family developed the property where they resided while the others bought land specifically to divide it into building lots. Hitchcock. Hitchcock had a flair for publicity and innovative sales techniques. Once the area had been surveyed and 972 plots laid out, he organized excursions from the city, hired brass bands to play, and gave prospects free lunch. The first sales event took place on February 18, 1869. Hitchcock priced empty lots at $300. Employing an innovative sales technique, he sold them on the installment plan. Purchasers made a down payment and owed $10 a month until the note was paid off. He took a 25% commission on each sale. To entice purchasers he sold lottery tickets with first option on choice lots as one set of prizes. Other prizes included option to purchase one of five houses already built on the property. It may have been he or perhaps Kelly who gave the name "Woodside" to the area. A member of the Kelly family, John A. F. This network continued to expand and Woodside evolved as a hub for railroad (the [[Main Line (Long Island Rail Road)|Long Island Rail Road's Main Line electrified]] in 1908), elevated [[rapid transit]] (the joint [[IRT Flushing Line|IRT/BRT Corona and Woodside Line]], 1917), and electrified trolleys (Newtown Railway Company, 1895, and [[New York and Queens County Railway|New York and Queens County Line]], 1896). With the incorporation of Queens into New York City in 1898 and subsequent passage of legislation mandating a five-cent citywide [[New York City transit fares|transit fare]] in 1904, Woodside residents had both abundant and inexpensive options for rapid public transportation. The commute was cheap and short, and during rush hours, the five-cent trip took as little as eight minutes to [[Times Square (IRT Flushing Line)|Times Square]]. Although other areas of Queens benefited from the expansion of cheap transit, Woodside was, back then, the only village in Queens with both railroad and rapid transit stations in addition to trolley lines. A second circumstance aiding the influx of upwardly-mobile low-income residents was a dramatic increase in local employment prospects. Although cheap, fast, and convenient transit made it possible for workers from Queens to have other-borough jobs, intra-borough employment opportunities were increasingly a realistic option. The waterside regions of Queens had long had substantial industries and businesses that benefited from access to water-borne transport. These commercial establishments multiplied as rail transportation became increasingly available and, in a virtuous growth cycle, as more prospective employees moved into the borough.{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1912/10/27/archives/builders-active-in-borough-of-queens-opening-of-through-electric.html |title=Builders Active in Borough of Queens. Much of its congregation and all its early pastors were of German nationality.Blessed Virgin Mary Help of Christians 1854–1954 [1954, unpaginated] The first church in Woodside proper, St. Paul's Protestant Episcopal, showed the dominant faith of the area's oldest and most prominent residents. It was established in 1874 by the families of landowners who had farmed there from its earliest settlement as well as by the estate-owning Germanic families that had moved in during the middle decades of the 19th century, including the longstanding Rapelye, Hicks, and Riker families and the newly arrived Sussdorf, Windmuller, and Kelly families. St. Paul's originally had a small congregation of only 50, with twice that in 1900; the Baptist church had about the same. St. Sebastian, this section's first Roman Catholic church, served a considerably larger population upon its 1896 foundation. The number of church members, originally 300, quickly grew and was reported to be 1,000 in 1902. Three representative examples are Woodside Apartments built in 1913, the [[Metropolitan Life Insurance Company]]'s project of 1922, and the projects of the Woodside Development Corporation in 1923. Located near the rail and rapid transit stations, the Woodside Apartments was a row of four-story, semi-detached buildings. There were four apartments on a floor, most of them having four rooms. Rents initially ranged from $18 to $20 a month. Located just as close to the trains, but on the other side of the village, the Metropolitan Life apartment project was more ambitious. Consisting of ten five-story buildings, the project had space for four hundred families.{{cite news |url=https://query.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=FB0915FB345D1A7A93C6A9178AD95F468285F9 |title=Latest Dealings in Realty Field. Latest Dealings in Realty Field. Part of Housing Program. Trading Indicated Strong Demand for Apartment House Properties in Manhattan |date=November 4, 1922 |work=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331}} The Woodside Development Corporation built four-story apartments with stores on the ground floor and both two- and one-family houses on two large plots of land near the center of the village.{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1923/09/08/archives/a-6000000-development-new-corporation-buys-queens-acreage-for.html |title=A$6,000,000 DEVELOPMENT.; New Corporation Buys Queens Acreage for Improvement With Homes. |date=September 8, 1923 |work=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 |access-date=2019-07-08 |language=en-US |archive-date=July 8, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190708173801/https://www.nytimes.com/1923/09/08/archives/a-6000000-development-new-corporation-buys-queens-acreage-for.html |url-status=live }} When a citywide aerial survey was taken in 1924, Woodside was shown to have quite a few other multifamily apartment buildings and duplexes along with its many small single-family homes.{{cite book |url=http://digitalgallery.nypl.org/nypldigital/id?1532593 |title=Sectional aerial maps of the City of New York / [photographed and assembled under the direction of the chief engineer, July 1st, 1924]. |last=Fairchild Aerial Camera Corporation |publisher=Bureau of Engineering, City of New York}} During the 1930s and into the post-war era, Woodside residential development continued to grow, although more slowly than in the boom years following World War I. In 1936, a last large tract of undeveloped land was made available for construction of garden apartments when a portion of the 10-acre Windmuller Estate was sold to developers.{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1941/07/16/archives/large-site-is-bought-for-suites-in-queens-gardentype-apartments-to.html |title=LARGE SITE IS BOUGHT FOR SUITES IN QUEENS; Garden-Type Apartments to Rise in Woodside Area |date=July 16, 1941 |work=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 |access-date=2019-07-08 |language=en-US |archive-date=July 8, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190708173205/https://www.nytimes.com/1941/07/16/archives/large-site-is-bought-for-suites-in-queens-gardentype-apartments-to.html |url-status=live }}{{cite news |title=Woodside Housing To Cost $4,000,000. The area still had few apartment buildings and very little industry. Although the rapid population growth of the 1920s had fallen off in the 1930s, the authors of the profile expected improved transit (the [[IND Queens Boulevard Line]] which opened in 1933) and a new shopping center to draw larger numbers of new residents. The complex consists of 20 six-story buildings with 1,358 apartments. It is located in western Woodside, bordering Astoria, between 49th and 51st Streets, 31st Avenue and Newtown Road.{{cite web |url=http://www.nyc.gov/html/nycha/html/developments/queenswoodside.shtml |title=WOODSIDE HOUSES |website=nyc.gov |publisher=[[New York City Housing Authority]] |access-date=November 13, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151112145304/http://www.nyc.gov/html/nycha/html/developments/queenswoodside.shtml |archive-date=November 12, 2015 |url-status=dead }} ===21st century=== At the turn of the 21st century, Woodside was finally seen to be built up. The neighborhood nonetheless continued to be seen as an attractive place to live—characterized by "wide avenues, leafy streets and a mix of private homes, small apartment buildings and the occasional towering co-op."{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2009/10/25/nyregion/25stop.html |title=Where Two Neighborhoods Meet, Straightforward Charm |last=Saltzstein |first=Dan |date=October 22, 2009 |work=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 |access-date=2019-07-08 |language=en-US |archive-date=July 8, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190708173208/https://www.nytimes.com/2009/10/25/nyregion/25stop.html |url-status=live }} The population was about 1,800 in 1880; 3,900 in 1900; 15,000 in 1920; and 41,000 in 1930.{{Cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1930/06/07/archives/1300-census-gain-in-jackson-heights-complete-figures-indicate-that.html |title=1,300% CENSUS GAIN IN JACKSON HEIGHTS; Complete Figures Indicate That Queens Community Is City's Fastest Growing Area. |archive-date=November 5, 2021 |title=Black Non-Hispanic Population NYC Neighborhood Tabulation Areas,* 2020|page=25|url-status=live}} ==Culture== ===Background=== The character of Woodside's population, in terms of national origin, has changed radically over time. Its first inhabitants were Native Americans, probably of the [[Mespeatches]], who gave their name to the town of Maspeth. The first European landowners were mainly Dutch and English and their laborers mainly British, African (slaves), and American Indian. During the nineteenth century, Germans largely took over from these first settlers. In addition to the major Germanic landowners already mentioned (the Kellys—whose name was originally Kölle—Riker, Schroeder, Schmidt, Sussdorf, and Windmuller), the first purchasers of Hitchcock's little plots were largely of German extraction. They included men with names like Eberhardt, Groeber, and Schlepergrel. Beginning at the close of the 19th century and through most of the 20th, growing numbers of Irish residents arrived and Woodside eventually became Irish enough to earn the nickname "Irishtown".{{Cite web |url=http://ps229woodside.wikispaces.com/4-Who+Lives+in+Woodside%3F+ |title=Who Lives in Woodside? |publisher=PS 229 Woodside |access-date=February 9, 2013}}{{cite news |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1990/08/13/nyregion/changing-city-woodside-queens-new-accents-old-brogue-quietly-reshape-woodside.html |title=The Changing City; Woodside, Queens; New Accents and Old Brogue Quietly Reshape Woodside |author=Joseph P. Fried |date=August 13, 1990 |work=The New York Times |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=May 12, 2016 |access-date=February 23, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160512081945/http://www.nytimes.com/1990/08/13/nyregion/changing-city-woodside-queens-new-accents-old-brogue-quietly-reshape-woodside.html |url-status=live }}{{cite news |title=From a Babel of Tongues, a Neighborhood: THE NEWCOMERS. The World Comes to Woodside |author=Susan Sachs |date=December 26, 1999 |work=The New York Times|issn=0362-4331}} A major turning point in the transition from German to Irish occurred in 1901 when the Greater New York Irish Athletic Association formally opened a large athletic complex called Celtic Park on the border between Woodside and Laurel Hill, its neighbor to the south.{{Cite web |url=http://www.wingedfist.com/Celtic_Park_History.html |title=A Brief History of Celtic Park |author=Ian McGowan |publisher=Winged Fist Organization |access-date=February 3, 2013 |archive-date=February 25, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20140225084941/http://www.wingedfist.com/Celtic_Park_History.html |url-status=live }} A second turning point was the death of Louis Windmuller, the last of the German estate owners. Prominent in local as well as city and national affairs, he was called the "grand old man" or "patriarch" of Woodside.{{cite journal |date=April 30, 1910 |title=Patriarch Saves His Lawn |journal=New York Daily Tribune}}{{cite journal |date=February 7, 1913 |title=Notables Who Walk |journal=Brooklyn Daily Star}} Although the estate did not go out of his heirs' hands until the close of the Depression and beginning of World War II, his passing nonetheless helps mark Woodside's transition from country village to suburban bedroom community.{{cite news |title=Mathews Buys Large Tract in Woodside; Windmuller Property; Last Large Vacant Plot in Section |date=September 27, 1942 |journal=Brooklyn Daily Star}}{{cite news |title=Old Windmuller Tract, Woodside, Urged for Park; Wooded Tract Offers Ideal Site, Resident Points Out |date=July 22, 1929 |journal=Brooklyn Daily Star}}{{Cite web |url=http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/Q031/history |title=Windmuller Park |work=Historical Signs Project |publisher=City of New York Parks & Recreation |access-date=March 23, 2013 |archive-date=January 17, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130117023603/http://www.nycgovparks.org/parks/Q031/history |url-status=live }} With large-scale [[residential development]] in the 1860s, Woodside became the largest [[Irish American]] community in Queens. In the early 1930s, the area was approximately 80% Irish.{{cite book |title=The New York Irish |last1=Baylor |first1=Ronald H. |last2=Meagher |first2=Timothy J. |publisher=Johns Hopkins University Press |year=1996 |isbn=0-8018-5199-8 |location=Baltimore |page=[https://archive.org/details/newyorkirish00bayorich/page/414 414] |url-access=registration |url=https://archive.org/details/newyorkirish00bayorich/page/414 }} A subsequent influx of Irish occurred during the 1980s and into the early 1990s when many Irish immigrated to New York due to poor economic conditions in Ireland. Many of these "new Irish" settled in Woodside, where the men found work as construction workers or bartenders while the women worked as waitresses, nannies or domestics. Toward the end of the 20th century, Irish dominance gradually yielded to a mixture of other nationalities, but even as the neighborhood has seen growth in ethnic diversity today, the area still retains a strong Irish American presence, and there continue to be a number of Irish pubs and restaurants scattered across Woodside. After World War II, families in the area were primarily of [[Irish people|Irish]], [[Italians|Italian]], and [[Jewish]] descent. Gradually, Dominicans and other nationalities began to make an appearance in the community, beginning in the late 1960s. A trend of diversity began then, and has continued since. This diversity has been remarked upon by many observers and can be shown in residents' places of worship. For example, the [[Winfield Reformed Church]] began in 1880 as a Dutch Calvinist church and in 1969 became the first Taiwanese congregation in America. Others of Woodside's places of worship now include ones that are [[Hindu]], Thai [[Buddhist]], [[Romanian Orthodox]], Filipino, Korean, Chinese, and Bahraini. Woodside has a strong Muslim community and is home of a large, multipurpose organization, the Islamic Institute of New York. Among St. Sebastian Mass-goers, a priest reports that are about 45% are Hispanic (particularly from Colombia and Mexico), 25% Irish, 25% Filipino, and 5% Korean.{{Cite web |url=http://www.hsj.org/modules/ask_a_pro/article.cfm?ArticleId=193 |title=Immigrants and Religion: Spirit of Home in House of God: Faith keeps immigrant groups together |author=Mae Cheng |year=2001 |work=my.hsj.org |publisher=ASNE, 209 Reynolds Journalism Institute |access-date=February 9, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120722175101/http://www.hsj.org/modules/ask_a_pro/article.cfm?ArticleId=193 |archive-date=July 22, 2012 |url-status=dead }} In 1999, Woodsiders came from 49 countries and spoke 34 different languages.{{cite news |url=https://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052748703523604575605171704881804 |title=Tastes on Woodside Avenue |author=Kavita Mokha |date=November 12, 2010 |work=The Wall Street Journal |archive-date=March 14, 2016 |access-date=August 8, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160314114741/http://www.wsj.com/articles/SB10001424052748703523604575605171704881804 |url-status=live }} In the early 1990s, many [[Asian American]] families moved into the area, particularly east of the [[61st Street – Woodside (IRT Flushing Line)|61st Street – Woodside]] subway station. In 2000, Woodside's population was 30% [[Asian American]]. Woodside has a large population of [[Thai Americans]], [[Korean Americans]], [[Chinese Americans]] and [[Filipino American]]s (see [[Koreatown]], [[Chinatown]], and [[Little Manila]]), each with their own respective [[New York City ethnic enclaves|ethnic enclave]]. There are also [[South Asian]] Americans, particularly [[Indian Americans]], [[Bangladeshi American]]s, [[Nepalese Americans]], and [[Pakistani Americans]], as well as a large [[Dominican people (Dominican Republic)|Dominican]] and [[Hispanic and Latino Americans|Latino]] population.{{cite news |url=http://www.nydailynews.com/real_estate/2009/08/14/2009-08-14_think_nyc_isnt_affordable_check_out_woodside.html |title=Think NYC isn't affordable? Check out Woodside |last=Sheftell |first=Jason |date=August 14, 2009 |newspaper=Daily News |access-date=August 19, 2009 |location=New York |archive-date=August 17, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090817111538/http://www.nydailynews.com/real_estate/2009/08/14/2009-08-14_think_nyc_isnt_affordable_check_out_woodside.html |url-status=live }} Reflecting its longtime diverse foods and drink, the neighborhood is filled with many cultural restaurants and pubs. It is also home to some of the city's most popular Thai, Filipino, Colombian, and Ecuadorian eateries. Woodside's diversity lends itself to a number of festivals and street fairs. It commemorates [[Saint Patrick's Day]] with a parade prior to the famous celebration in Manhattan. Woodside also hosts several events in the summer, including an [[Independence Day (United States)|Independence Day]] street fair. ===Little Manila=== [[File:KrystalCafe JohnnyAirCargo WoodsideQueensNY Commons.JPG|thumb|300px|right|Woodside's [[Little Manila#Woodside, Queens|Little Manila]] on [[Roosevelt Avenue]]]] {{Further|Filipinos in the New York City metropolitan region}} "[[Little Manila]]", or Filipinotown, stretches from 63rd-71st Streets on Roosevelt Avenue, where many Filipino-owned businesses have flocked to serve Woodside's large [[Filipino American]] community; the neighborhood is known for its concentration of Filipinos.{{cite news |url=http://www.gmanetwork.com/news/story/210966/pinoyabroad/little-manila-rises-in-new-york-city-s-queens-borough |title=Little Manila rises in New York City's Queens borough |last=Marquez |first=Liaa |date=January 19, 2011 |newspaper=GMA News |access-date=November 26, 2014 |quote=Previously an Irish neighborhood, Woodside has grown to be one of the most diverse areas in the city. Amid Mexican-, Indian-, and Korean-owned stores lies a hefty sampling of the Philippines. The area now serves as home to the rising population of Filipinos in the city. |archive-date=July 6, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150706062701/http://www.gmanetwork.com/news/story/210966/pinoyabroad/little-manila-rises-in-new-york-city-s-queens-borough |url-status=live }} Filipino cafés and restaurants dominate the area, as well as several freight and remittance centers scattered throughout the neighborhood. Other Filipino-owned businesses including professional services (medical, dental, [[optometry|optical]]), driving schools, beauty salons, immigration services, and video rental places providing the latest movies from the Philippines dot the community. This area attracts many local Filipinos and non-Filipinos alike and from neighboring places of [[Long Island]], [[Connecticut]], [[Pennsylvania]], and [[New Jersey]]. In February 2008, the Bayanihan Filipino Community Center opened its doors in Woodside, a project spearheaded by the Philippine Forum. The Philippine Forum also hosts the annual Bayanihan Cultural Festival at the Hart Playground in September in commemoration of Filipino American History Month.{{cite web |url=http://www.philippineforum.org/2012/09/27/fourth-annual-bayanihan-cultural-festival-back-to-where-it-all-began/ |title=Fourth Annual Bayanihan Cultural Festival: Back to Where It All Began |date=September 27, 2012 |publisher=Philippine Forum |access-date=December 1, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150506230517/http://www.philippineforum.org/2012/09/27/fourth-annual-bayanihan-cultural-festival-back-to-where-it-all-began/ |archive-date=May 6, 2015 |url-status=dead }} The intersection of 70th Street and Roosevelt Avenue was co-named "Little Manila Avenue" on June 12, 2022, with a sign-unveiling ceremony to celebrate the Filipino community's growing presence and contributions in Queens.{{Cite web |date=May 27, 2022 |title=Woodside Street Corner to Be Co-Named "Little Manila Avenue" Next Month in Celebration of Filipino Community |url=https://sunnysidepost.com/woodside-street-corner-to-be-co-named-little-manila-avenue-next-month-in-celebration-of-filipino-community |access-date=2022-06-12 |website=Sunnyside Post |language=en-US}} Concomitantly, there is also a Roosevelt Avenue in [[Roosevelt Avenue, Quezon City|Quezon City, Philippines]]. The corner in Queens was co-named "Little Manila Avenue". === St. Patrick's Day Parade === [[File:WAG2284 (48838552297).jpg|thumb|alt=|The Green Man, St. Pat's for All Parade]] Woodside hosts New York City's only [[Saint Patrick's Day]] parade that invites members of New York City's LGBTQ Irish community to march; it is called the [[St. Pat's for All|St. Pat's for All Parade]].{{cite web |url=http://www.stpatsforall.com/ |title=St. Pat's for All: Home |website=St. Pat's for All |access-date=November 13, 2015}} The parade was founded by LGBTQ+ rights activist [[Brendan Fay]] after the Irish Lesbian and Gay Organization (ILGO) was repeatedly denied permission to march in the Manhattan St. Patrick's Day parade by the [[Ancient Order of Hibernians]].{{Cite web|url=http://www.nyclgbtsites.org/site/starting-point-of-first-st-pats-for-all-parade/|title=St. Pat's for All Parade|website=NYC LGBT Historic Sites Project|language=en-US|access-date=October 17, 2019}} The parade runds from Sunnyside to Woodside, with its starting point in 43rd Street and Skillman Avenue. ==== History of St. Pat's for All ==== [[File:WAG2377 (48838005373).jpg|thumb|The people marching at the St. Patrick's for All Parade 2018|alt=|left|219x219px]] In 1991, the recently established gay and lesbian Irish organization ILGO was denied permission to march in the St. Patrick's Day Parade on Fifth Avenue. When New York City Mayor Dinkins intervened on their behalf, ILGO members were allowed to march for that one time, but their presence was received with hostility from other marchers as well as the spectators, who openly hurled abuse at them and doused with beer.Mulligan, Adrian. "Parading Possibility : "St. Pat's for All" and the Re-imagining of Irishness." Irish-American Gay, Lesbian, and Bisexual Group of Boston]] that private citizens organizing a public demonstration may not be compelled by the state to include groups who impart a message the organizers do not want to be presented by their demonstration.{{Cite web|url=http://www.irishcentral.com/news/politics/Timeline-of-the-NYC-St-Patricks-Day-Parades-LGBT-controversy-PHOTO--VIDEO.html|title=Timeline of NYC St. Patrick's Day Parade's LGBT controversy|date=March 17, 2018|website=IrishCentral.com|language=en|access-date=2019-10-17|archive-date=February 16, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160216150013/http://www.irishcentral.com/news/politics/Timeline-of-the-NYC-St-Patricks-Day-Parades-LGBT-controversy-PHOTO--VIDEO.html|url-status=live}} In the wake of these court rulings, Brendan Fay founds the [[Lavender and Green Alliance]] (LAG), which organizes an inclusive event "open to anybody who wished to celebrate the spirit of Irishness and their connections to Ireland" and name it "St. Pat's for All". A trolley barn at Northern Boulevard and 51st Street has been preserved as the Tower Square Shopping Center. The New York and Queens Railroad Company built the barn in 1896. A transportation hub like the LIRR/IRT stations, it was the largest car barn in Queens.{{Cite web |url=http://forgotten-ny.com/1998/09/woodsides-trolley-barn/ |title=Woodside's Trolley Barn |date=September 15, 1998 |publisher=Forgotten New York, in association with the Greater Astoria Historical Society (This was the very first Forgotten NY page — created September 15, 1998; rev. 3/12/12) |access-date=March 23, 2013 |archive-date=May 7, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130507110027/http://forgotten-ny.com/1998/09/woodsides-trolley-barn/ |url-status=live }} Woodside also possesses an ancient tree, not the great chestnut (which was gone by the end of the 19th century) but a large copper beech of somewhere between 150 and 300 years' age. Documents in the archive of the Queens Historical Society suggest that it might have been planted during the time of the Revolutionary War.{{Cite web |url=http://queensnyc.com/tag/ny-landmark-preservation-commission/ |title=Woodside locals want to landmark a giant beech tree |author=Meg Cotner |year=2012 |publisher=NYC Queens in Context |access-date=March 22, 2013 }}{{Dead link|date=January 2026 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}{{Cite web |url=http://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20121010/woodside/advocates-pushing-landmark-queens-tree-that-may-date-revolution |title=Tree That May Date to Revolution Deserves Landmark Status, Advocates Say |author=Ewa Kern-Jedrychowska |year=2012 |publisher=DNAinfo.com |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130512032744/http://www.dnainfo.com/new-york/20121010/woodside/advocates-pushing-landmark-queens-tree-that-may-date-revolution |archive-date=May 12, 2013 |url-status=dead |access-date=March 22, 2013}} Among the oldest of Woodside's historic landmarks are its cemeteries. [[Calvary Cemetery (Queens, New York)|Calvary Cemetery]] was founded in 1845 by trustees of Manhattan's St. Patrick's Cathedral for Roman Catholic burials and was later expanded by the addition of three sections comprising New Calvary.{{Cite web |url=http://forgotten-ny.com/2011/12/calvary-cemetery/ |title=Enjoy the Silence; Calvary Cemetery |year=2012 |publisher=Forgotten New York, in association with the Greater Astoria Historical Society |access-date=March 22, 2013 |archive-date=May 7, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130507122959/http://forgotten-ny.com/2011/12/calvary-cemetery/ |url-status=live }} Calvary and New Calvary's combined {{convert|300|acre|ha}} contain over three million burials.{{cite news |url=http://www.bklyn-genealogy-info.com/Cemetery/Calvary.hist.html |title=History of Calvary Cemetery |date=October 26, 1973 |journal=Catholic News, on the Brooklyn Genealogy Information Page |archive-date=February 20, 2009 |access-date=September 9, 2014 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090220134514/http://bklyn-genealogy-info.com/Cemetery/Calvary.hist.html |url-status=live }} Located on 54th Street between 31st & 32nd Avenues, the Moore-Jackson Cemetery is much older and smaller than Calvary. Established in 1733, it is one of the oldest cemeteries in New York. Only fifteen graves remain visible, the earliest dated 1769.{{Cite web |url=http://forgotten-ny.com/2005/10/woodside-queens-part-1/ |title=Woodside, Queens, Part 1 |author=Christina Wilkinson |year=2005 |publisher=Forgotten New York, in association with the Greater Astoria Historical Society |access-date=March 22, 2013 |archive-date=May 7, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130507114507/http://forgotten-ny.com/2005/10/woodside-queens-part-1/ |url-status=live }}{{Cite web |url=http://www.scoutingny.com/?tag=moore-jackson-cemetery |title=The Cemetery on the Old Farm...in Queens? |author=Nick Carr |year=2009 |access-date=March 22, 2013 |archive-date=February 2, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130202005933/http://www.scoutingny.com/?tag=moore-jackson-cemetery |url-status=live }} [[File:1 Bulova Avenue jeh.jpg|left|thumb|[[Bulova Corporation]] previous headquarters in Woodside]] The [[Bulova Corporation]] had its headquarters in northern Woodside along [[Interstate 278]] until 2014, when it sold the building for $30 million and relocated to the [[Empire State Building]].La Guerre, Liam. [https://qns.com/2014/10/watchmaker-bulova-selling-woodside-headquarters-for-30m/ "Watchmaker Bulova selling Woodside headquarters for $30M"], [[QNS.com]], October 16, 2014. Accessed February 5, 2026. "Bulova Corporation, a watch-making company, is selling its headquarters at 26-15 Brooklyn-Queens Expressway in Woodside for $30 million, according to a published report. The firm, which has owned the two-story office building since moving there in 1986, shifted a portion of its operations into a 33,000-square-foot space in the Empire State Building three months ago, Crain’s reported." The headquarters opened in 1875. Although few have been documented, some of Woodside's old buildings still remain in place. Of those for which information is available, Woodside's first church, St. Paul's Protestant Episcopal, holds pride of place. It was damaged by fire in 2007 but still stands in its original location. An article published on the [[Forgotten NY]] weblog in 2005 lists this and other interesting structures from 19th century Woodside which have survived. All are located close to the center of town. They include the Hook and Ladder Company (1884), the home of Otto Groeber and his family (1870), the Woodside Pavilion (1877), and Meyer's Hotel (1882). Another article on this blog shows structures from the early 20th century that are still standing.{{Cite web |url=http://forgotten-ny.com/2005/10/woodside-queens-part-2/ |title=Woodside, Queens, Part 2 |date=October 22, 2005 |publisher=Forgotten New York, in association with the Greater Astoria Historical Society |access-date=March 22, 2013 |archive-date=May 7, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130507123825/http://forgotten-ny.com/2005/10/woodside-queens-part-2/ |url-status=live }} In addition, the [[Winfield Reformed Church]] is located in Woodside. {{Clear}} ==Transportation== [[File:Boarding the New York City MTA 7 subway.png|thumb|[[61st Street–Woodside station]]]] The [[IRT Flushing Line]] ({{NYCS trains|Flushing}}) of the [[New York City Subway]] has stations at [[52nd Street (IRT Flushing Line)|52nd]] (local), [[61st Street – Woodside (IRT Flushing Line)|61st]] (express) and [[69th Street (IRT Flushing Line)|69th]] Streets (local) on Roosevelt Avenue; the [[IND Queens Boulevard Line]] local services ({{NYCS trains|Queens local}}) make stops at [[Northern Boulevard (IND Queens Boulevard Line)|Northern Boulevard]] and [[65th Street (IND Queens Boulevard Line)|65th Street]] along Broadway.{{cite web |url=http://web.mta.info/maps/submap.html |title=New York City Subway Map |publisher=[[Metropolitan Transportation Authority]] |access-date=December 23, 2014 |archive-date=September 18, 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180918074651/http://web.mta.info/maps/submap.html |url-status=live }} The [[Woodside (LIRR station)|Woodside]] station of the [[Long Island Rail Road|LIRR]] is connected to the 61st Street subway station. The {{NYC bus link|Q18|Q32|Q39|Q47|Q53 SBS|Q60|Q70 SBS|prose=y}} buses connect Woodside to the rest of Queens; the Q32 and Q60 run to [[Manhattan]], and the Q70 SBS goes to [[LaGuardia Airport]] via [[Jackson Heights–Roosevelt Avenue/74th Street station|Roosevelt Avenue/74th Street]].{{Cite NYC bus map|Q}} The [[Interstate 278|Brooklyn-Queens Expressway]] (I-278) is a major highway passing through the area, serving Woodside via exits 39 through 43, as is the Long Island Expressway (I-495) via exit 18.
